newsitem.title: USA: Knight-Ridder net rises on higher ad revenues.
newsitem.headline: Knight-Ridder net rises on higher ad revenues.

text.p: Newspaper publisher Knight-Ridder Inc. Thursday reported a 44 percent jump in income for the second quarter, bolstered by robust advertising revenues and a decline in newsprint prices.

The company said net income hit $61.3 million for the second quarter, up from $41.7 million in the year-ago period. Earnings per share rose to 61 cents from 43 cents a year ago, and were several cents above Wall Street analysts' projections.
Revenues climbed to $717.9 million, from $600 million a year ago.
The second-quarter results exclude the discontinued operation of Knight-Ridder Information Inc., which the company expects to sell in the third quarter of this year.
However, the figures include results from four newspapers the company purchased in May from The Walt Disney Co.
Excluding the Disney papers, Knight-Ridder's total advertising revenue rose 8 percent for the quarter, led by growth in classified ads.
Newsprint costs fell 29 percent in the same period.

The company's second-quarter performance mirrors gains by other big newspaper publishers. Strong advertising revenues helped boost earnings at The New York Times Co., Los Angeles Times publisher Times Mirror Co. and the Washington Post Co.
Excluding the Disney papers, Knight-Ridder's classified advertising rose 11.7 percent for the second quarter, with help wanted ads up 20.6 percent.

"We continue to anticipate an earnings increase for the year, despite dilution from the Disney acquisition, of at least 20 percent," Chief Financial Officer Ross Jones said in a statement accompanying the results.
He added that the company expects newsprint costs to remain steady into late 1997 or early 1998.

"Should there be an increase at either of those times, we will not feel the impact until 1998 -- leaving us confident that the cost of newsprint will be about 15 percent less this year than last," Jones said.
Miami-based Knight-Ridder publishes 35 daily newspapers in the United States, including The Miami Herald.
The company's stock was unchanged at $50 on the New York Stock Exchange at midday.
